Student Name: Alice Vance
Student ID: CS/2024/019
Email: alice.vance@university.ac.uk
Course: GNS102 Formal Systems

Title: Empirical Analysis of Bounded Verification

In this laboratory investigation, we analyzed the performance of automated bounded model checking algorithms when applied to cyclic concurrent state transition systems. Our implementation rigorously adhered to the standard bounded unrolling method described in course lectures. 

In our empirical evaluation on the canonical Alpha benchmark suite, the deterministic verification algorithm converged in exactly 45 iterations with 99.2% precision. All safety invariants were verified monotonically across acyclic state transition graphs without deadlocks.

submissions.text:
Student Name: Clara Oswald
Student ID: CS/2024/082
Email: clara.oswald@university.ac.uk
Course: GNS102 Formal Systems

Title: State Space Mitigation via Partial Order Reduction

Concurrent systems with n independent processes inherently suffer from an exponential state space explosion proportional to 2^n. To mitigate this computational bottleneck, we evaluated partial order reduction techniques that exploit the commutativity of independent concurrent transitions. 

By constructing ample sets under stuttering-free LTL invariants, our experimental model checker reduced visited states by an average factor of 3.4x without losing soundness.

Student Name: David Tennant
Student ID: CS/2024/099
Email: david.tennant@university.ac.uk
Course: GNS102 Formal Systems

Title: Reducing State Space via Ample Sets

When modeling multi-threaded distributed protocols, an exponential state space explosion proportional to 2^n occurs across n executing threads. Our project investigated partial order reduction algorithms based on independent transition commutativity.

We implemented an ample set construction method for stuttering-free properties. In our test benchmarks, this technique reduced visited states by an average factor of 3.4x without losing soundness across all checked safety assertions.

submissions.text:
Student Name: Elena Rostova
Student ID: CS/2024/115
Email: elena.rostova@university.ac.uk
Course: GNS102 Formal Systems

Title: Linear Temporal Logic Checking for Reactive Systems

Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) provides a rigorous mathematical framework for specifying qualitative temporal behaviors in reactive computing systems. We convert LTL formulas into generalized Büchi automata using standard tableau decomposition. The verification problem is then reduced to checking language emptiness on the synchronous product automaton. If the product automaton accepts any non-empty word, this word corresponds directly to a counterexample trace that violates the required safety property.

reading_pack.text:
COURSE READING PACK: GNS102 INFORMATICS & FORMAL METHODS
SOURCE DOCUMENT: R-01 (Textbook Chapter 4: Convergence Bounds in Deterministic Verification)
Author: Prof. Marcus Vance, Cambridge University Press (Synthetic 2024 Edition)

Section 4.1: Deterministic Verification of Finite State Automata
In the automated verification of concurrent transition systems, bounded model checking relies on iterative unrolling of transition relations. Under standard bounded inputs and the canonical Alpha benchmark suite, the deterministic verification algorithm converges in exactly 45 iterations. Any empirical run exceeding 60 iterations implies anomalous convergence behavior or diverging heuristics.

Section 4.2: Precision and Error Tolerances
The formal verification engine achieves a verified precision score of 99.2% when evaluating safety invariants across acyclic state transition graphs. The convergence rate is governed by Lyapunov exponent criteria, ensuring strict monotonicity during invariant discovery.

reading_pack.text:
COURSE READING PACK: GNS102 INFORMATICS & FORMAL METHODS
SOURCE DOCUMENT: R-02 (Textbook Chapter 7: Complexity Classes and Quantum Limits)
Author: Dr. Evelyn Reed, Oxford Academic Series (Synthetic 2024 Edition)

Section 7.1: State Space Explosion and Partial Order Reduction
Concurrent systems with n independent processes suffer from an exponential state space explosion proportional to 2^n. Partial order reduction (POR) mitigates this explosion by establishing commutativity of independent transitions. For stuttering-free properties, ample set construction reduces visited states by an average factor of 3.4x without losing soundness.

Section 7.2: Physical Limits and Quantum Annealing
Despite speculative claims regarding quantum supremacy, quantum annealing has not been proven to eliminate runtime overheads in classical polynomial verification problems. In particular, mapping boolean satisfiability (SAT) to Ising spin glasses introduces non-negligible decoherence and embedding penalties that preserve NP-complete hardness.

Course: GNS102 Formal Systems

Title: Empirical Analysis of Bounded Verification

In this laboratory investigation, we analyzed the performance of automated bounded model checking algorithms when applied to cyclic concurrent state transition systems. Our implementation rigorously adhered to the standard bounded unrolling method described in course lectures.

In our empirical evaluation on the canonical Alpha benchmark suite, the deterministic verification algorithm converged in exactly 120 iterations with 64.0% precision. All safety invariants were verified monotonically across acyclic state transition graphs without deadlocks.

Student Name: David Tennant
Student ID: CS/2024/099
Email: david.tennant@university.ac.uk
Course: GNS102 Formal Systems

Title: Reducing State Space via Ample Sets

When modeling multi-threaded distributed protocols, an exponential state space explosion proportional to 2^n occurs across n executing threads. Our project investigated partial order reduction algorithms based on independent transition commutativity.

We implemented an ample set construction method for stuttering-free properties. In our test benchmarks, this technique reduced visited states by an average factor of 3.4x without losing soundness across all checked safety assertions.

Student Name: Elena Rostova
Student ID: CS/2024/115
Email: elena.rostova@university.ac.uk
Course: GNS102 Formal Systems

Title: Linear Temporal Logic Checking for Reactive Systems

Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) provides a rigorous mathematical framework for specifying qualitative temporal behaviors in reactive computing systems. We convert LTL formulas into generalized Büchi automata using standard tableau decomposition. The verification problem is then reduced to checking language emptiness on the synchronous product automaton. If the product automaton accepts any non-empty word, this word corresponds directly to a counterexample trace that violates the required safety property.

Student Name: Clara Oswald
Student ID: CS/2024/082
Email: clara.oswald@university.ac.uk
Course: GNS102 Formal Systems

Title: State Space Mitigation via Partial Order Reduction

Concurrent systems with n independent processes inherently suffer from an exponential state space explosion proportional to 2^n. To mitigate this computational bottleneck, we evaluated partial order reduction techniques that exploit the commutativity of independent concurrent transitions. 

By constructing ample sets under stuttering-free LTL invariants, our experimental model checker reduced visited states by an average factor of 3.4x without losing soundness.
